item.title: One brick at a time: How Monumental uses robotics to build walls
item.dc:creator: Mike Oitzman
item.description:
CEO Salar al Khafaji introduces podcast listeners to how Monumental is using robotics to build walls.

The post One brick at a time: How Monumental uses robotics to build walls appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The Robot Report Podcast · One brick at a time: How Monumental uses robotics to build walls

Salar al Khafaji, founder and CEO of Monumental.

In Episode 261 of The Robot Report Podcast, we learn about “Walls as a Service” and the emerging construction opportunity for robotics and automation.

Our guest is Salar al Khafaji, founder and CEO of Monumental. A recognized leader at the intersection of AI, robotics, and the built environment, he is focused on bringing scalable automation to construction, one of the world’s largest and least digitized industries, by making it software-defined and hardware-enabled.

Previously, al Kafaji co-founded the data visualization platform Silk, which Palantir Technologies acquired in 2016.

Be sure to catch our prior coverage this week of Monumental.

item.title: Learn how AVs and robotics are laying the groundwork for field deployments at RoboBusiness
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
ASI CEO Mel Torrie will explore why the intersection of autonomous vehicles and robotics will further revolutionize field deployments.

The post Learn how AVs and robotics are laying the groundwork for field deployments at RoboBusiness appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
ASI is providing autonomy to existing field equipment. Source; Autonomous Solutions Inc.

Today’s autonomous vehicle fleets are successfully addressing pain points in geographically remote or rugged locations. Everyday, the technology is improving worker safety and operational efficiency. But, in the next 10 years, we’ll see a massive leap forward in field robotics, according to Mel Torrie, the founder and CEO of Autonomous Solutions Inc., or ASI.

The use of mobile robotics in outdoor applications is poised to advance significantly over the decade. To unlock the next level of productivity, developers must design autonomous vehicles to support that integration and foster collaborative relationships among platforms.

At RoboBusiness, ASI‘s Torrie will lead the session, “Designing the Robotics Ecosystem for Outdoor Autonomy.” He will explore why the intersection of autonomous vehicles and advanced robotics will further revolutionize field deployments.

Torrie will also share insights on how building a unified, cooperative ecosystem where physical robotics seamlessly accompany and work alongside autonomous vehicles will compound operational benefits. Attendees will gain a strategic roadmap for navigating this shifting landscape, learning how the symbiosis of rugged vehicle platforms and intelligent robotics will redefine predictable productivity and safety in the world’s most challenging work environments.

Meet field robotics veteran Mel Torrie

Mel Torrie is a global leader in vendor-agnostic vehicle automation. With over two decades of robotics leadership, he has pioneered autonomous technologies across the mining, agriculture, construction, and logistics industries.

Torrie grew up on a farm in Alberta, Canada, which motivated him to get an education and automate his tractors. He earned an MS degree in electrical engineering at Utah State University and began robotics research 28 years ago.

Torrie and his team founded ASI in 2000 and have bootstrapped the company through partnerships with the world’s largest field robotics OEMs.

item.title: How to select the right rack and pinion system for high-precision linear motion
item.dc:creator: Sana Kazilbash
item.description:
GAM explains why robotics designers should consider pinion size when thinking about motion control for high-precision applications.

The post How to select the right rack and pinion system for high-precision linear motion appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Sponsored by GAM.

GAM rack, pinion, and gearbox systems are optimized for high performance in all the components. (Image: GAM.)

Picture a scissor car jack — the one in your trunk for changing a tire. The spinning motion as you turn the crank translates to the linear motion as the jack rises.

This is how a rack and pinion system works. The spinning part is the pinion, a gear that receives the rotational input. The toothed part being pushed along is the rack, a long bar with gear teeth that the pinion rides against. Depending on the application, either the rack moves back and forth while the pinion stays in place, or the rack stays fixed and whatever the pinion is attached to travels back and forth (or up and down).

It is important to select the right rack and pinion system, as a wrong decision can impact both performance and cost.

“If you go too small with your rack and pinion, it can break,” says Matt Ruggles, senior design engineer at GAM, a U.S.-based manufacturer of servo gear reducers and other motion control components. “If you go too large, you might run into space constraints, and you’ll be paying for more rack and pinion than you need.”

The pinion size relative to the rack has to be matched so the system can reach the required speed and deliver the necessary feed force. The overall size of the rack and pinion also plays into inertia matching between the motor and load, which affects how smoothly the system moves.

So, how does the selection process work?

“Usually when people are putting together a rack and pinion system, their primary concern is either speed or feed force, and so you start with that requirement and kind of work backwards,” says Ruggles.

When feed force is the priority, that means making sure the rack is big enough to transmit the required force, and that the pinion is sized to match the motor or gearbox driving it. Similarly, when speed takes precedence, the rack and pinion are selected to allow the system to reach the target speed based on the motor or gearbox input.

Sometimes the process runs in the other direction. If a customer already has a motor selected, sizing can start from that motor’s speed and the positioning accuracy needed. Applications that need better positional accuracy may call for a higher-precision rack.

From there, tooth size and shape come into play. “The larger the rack, the bigger and stronger the teeth,” says Ruggles. “A higher tooth quality is going to run quieter usually and will offer better linear positioning, be more accurate.”

Another consideration is whether the teeth are straight or helical. Helical teeth are cut at an angle so they engage progressively, producing smoother, quieter motion and slightly more strength. Straight teeth engage all at once, making the motion rougher and noisier by comparison. While there’s very little cost difference between the two, helical teeth do introduce an axial force on the pinion and rack, perpendicular to the direction of motion.

A gearbox, pinion, and rack system provide the 7th axis, or lateral movement, for an articulated robot. Credit: GAM

Pinion size plays a significant role as well. Smaller pinions are preferred for high-precision applications; for any rotational error or backlash in the gearbox or motor, the impact on linear position is a lot smaller.

“With a smaller pinion, the lost motion through your system has less of an effect on how that overall positioning works in a linear fashion, versus a large pinion which can almost amplify that slop in the system,” says Ruggles.

A smaller pinion also transmits torque more effectively and requires less of it from the motor and gearbox to deliver the same feed force, allowing for smaller, less expensive components. The higher ratio further improves inertia matching between the motor and load.

The downside is that the maximum speed the system can achieve is going to be a lot lower, or the motor and gearbox will have to spin much faster to compensate. When speed matters more than precision, a larger pinion covers more distance per rotation.

Once the rack and pinion are selected, that drives gearbox choice, which then determines motor sizing.

One consistent mistake Ruggles sees engineers making is sizing the system around only one variable — feed force, for example — and not accounting for others until it’s too late.

“All of a sudden, they need to go up a rack size, get a bigger gearbox, and suddenly everything’s doubled in cost,” says Ruggles.

The same happens with inertia: correcting a mismatch by increasing the gearbox ratio reduces output speed, which cascades back through the whole system.

GAM’s engineers can help with the selection of various components in rack and pinion systems.

“We have sizing software where the customer can give us their feed force, speed, moving mass, and we can calculate the gearbox size, motor size, inertia matching,” says Ruggles. “As we’re sizing all those things, we have different size racks that we can offer, different size pinions to go with those racks, and then a variety of different gearboxes that we can match with those pinions, to really optimize the system.”

To learn more, visit GAM.

The post How to select the right rack and pinion system for high-precision linear motion appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: How drone developers are navigating changing regulatory landscapes to help farmers
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Before the FCC put restrictions on foreign-made robots, it had already set similar restrictions on drones last year, noted Hylio.

The post How drone developers are navigating changing regulatory landscapes to help farmers appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Hylio offers a range of drones that use digital flowmeters to spray fields at precise dosages. | Source: Hylio

Earlier this year, the Federal Communication Commission threw much of the robotics industry into uncertainty when it announced new limits on imports of certain robots from foreign countries. For those building and operating drones such as Hylio, this is a familiar story.

In December 2025, the FCC added foreign-made drones and U.S.-assembled drones with major foreign-made parts, to its Covered List. This list includes companies and technologies that the commission has prohibited. Arthur Erickson, the co-founder and CEO of agricultural drone developer Hylio, said the news didn’t come as a surprise for him.

Erickson launched the Richmond, Texas-based company in 2015. Even then, he saw that China had a clear advantage in the drone market. This is why he made manufacturing in the U.S. as much as possible a priority.

“There was part of me that knew that was going to be a problem,“ Erickson told The Robot Report. “Back in 2015, you had to have stuff from China, because that was the only country making it. So, within reason, we thought, ‘What could we make in house as a company?’”

If the team couldn’t build components in-house, the next best option was finding a domestic or ally manufacturer.

“That’s a core tenet of our philosophy for our supply chain, way before it was officially on any sort of legal radar or in the zeitgeist of the industry, so to speak,” Erickson said. “That means that we’re really well positioned right now. Now that it’s become a legal reality and a huge push by the U.S. government to completely make the U.S. drone supply chain domestically independent, we’re well ahead of our peers because we’ve always focused on that.”

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Hylio helps farmers navigate changing drone regulations

Erickson said the current regulatory landscape is one of the biggest challenges drone producers and users are facing today. Right now, to operate a drone, a user needs to navigate a mix of federal and local regulations that could change at a moment’s notice.

“It’s not usually the case for any product or equipment that you need to do three or four different licenses first before you can use it,” Erickson said.

To navigate this, users need to have honest conversations with their technology provider, he explained.

“Make sure you have all the legal stuff in place, because especially right now, there’s a lot of change in terms of the way that these drones are regulated and licensed by the FCC and the FAA and so on,” said Erickson. “Where your drone comes from matters. When you’re talking to dealers, distributors, whoever, when you’re in the market, ask these questions, and make sure you get a real answer.”

Some providers, like Hylio, provide their customers with a guide for how to navigate the process and help customers understand which licenses they need to apply for. “Make sure you have all of your licenses in place before you actually start doing any real commercial operations,” Erickson said.

Planned, phased deployments can yield strong results

Despite the challenges, drones can still provide real value for farmers. But it’s key for users to have a realistic understanding of what the process will look like. In agriculture, some users are already well positioned for deploying drones.

“We’ve had people come in that have a background in aerial application by helicopter and planes, so they are very regimented and disciplined,” noted Erickson. “They understand the importance of having safety checklists and SOPs clearly defined for their team,” Erickson said.

So what can we learn from these customers? Having a plan is key, Erickson said. It allows users to get the most value from their drones the fastest.

“Think about where you’re going to apply it. Chances are, it’s probably not on 100% of your land. Maybe you start off with 20% of your land that’s traditionally trickier to access with the tractors you have,” he said. “Put it where it’s needed first. Then, as you get more experience with it, and grow your fleet by a few more drones, you can start treating more and more and replacing more and more of the traditional methods on your land.”

Farmers need more automation, says Erickson

Erickson has more than a decade of experience working with farmers and hearing about their frustrations first hand. This has shown him how desperately the industry needs automation.

Across the board, Erickson said he sees the same story. Prices for certain crops, particularly grain, soybeans, and wheat, have been steadily dropping for years. In some cases, such as corn, prices have dropped 50% to 70% in recent years, said Erickson.

“All the while, their costs are dramatically increasing by basically the same figure,” he said about the farmers. “So, a 50% to 60% cost increase from pre-COVID, 2019 levels.”

Fertilizers are a big part of this, but the problem also extends to pesticides, herbicides, and other things that farmers need to ship from abroad. Between COVID-19, the Russia-Ukraine conflict, trade wars, and the conflict with Iran, Erickson said the industry has grown increasingly stressed.

“All these political and geostrategic conflicts have really disrupted the global supply chain and really just increased these input costs for farmers,” he said. “They’re getting squeezed from both ends. They’re not making as much money per acre, per bushel, and they’re spending lot more. That’s just not a recipe for a lot of financial success for them.”

In response to these challenges, Erickson said Hylio hopes to come in and show farmers how they can do more with less.

“If you can only afford half of the inputs you used to put into your crop, can you make that amount of chemical more effective? Can you meet or exceed the effectiveness of your previous treatments at higher volumes by using precise targeted attacks on the fungus that’s affecting your corn or the insects?” he asked. “Whatever the pathogen is that’s affecting your crops, can you be smarter and reduce the input amount that you need and get the same, if not better, results?”

The post How drone developers are navigating changing regulatory landscapes to help farmers appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Teradyne Robotics sues JAKA over 3 Universal Robots patents
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
New details reveal the lawsuit involves three Universal Robots patents about robot interfaces, safety brakes, and joints.

The post Teradyne Robotics sues JAKA over 3 Universal Robots patents appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Collaborative robot arms from JAKA Robotics (left) and Universal Robots.

JAKA Robotics asked last week where the Teradyne Robotics lawsuit was. Well, safe to say JAKA found it.

The Unified Patent Court (UPC) docket shows Teradyne filed its patent infringement case against JAKA Robotics GmbH on Aug. 24, 2026 – three days before Teradyne Robotics publicly announced the lawsuit.

Teradyne Robotics A/S, which owns Universal Robots, is accusing JAKA’s German subsidiary of infringing the patents. Teradyne previously said the case covers both hardware and software and a broad range of JAKA collaborative robots sold in Europe. Teradyne is the world’s leading developer of collaborative robot arms, having sold more than 100,000 robots since it was founded in 2005.

3 patents involved

The case, UPC-CFI-0003057/2026, was filed in the UPC’s Copenhagen Local Division and centers on three Universal Robots patents:

EP1996376 | Programmable Robot and User Interface: covers a programmable robot system and user interface, including a touchscreen that displays a 3D representation of the robot and allows operators to control its movements. Read patent

EP3045273 | Joint for a Robot: covers a robot-joint safety brake involving a solenoid, ratchet and annular friction member associated with the motor axle. Additional claims cover encoder arrangements and other joint features. Read patent

EP3530420 | Joint for a Robot: covers aspects of robot-joint construction, including output flanges and structures connecting adjacent joints. Read patent

All three patents have a March 2006 priority date and are assigned to Universal Robots. The public docket does not yet show which specific JAKA cobot models Teradyne Robotics alleges infringe which patent claims, but both companies offer a larger variety of options.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

JAKA questioned the lawsuit

After Teradyne Robotics announced the case on Aug. 27, JAKA said it had not received official notification or communication from Teradyne Robotics. The company said it was seeking details about the allegations and pointed to two previous Freedom-to-Operate analyses that it said found no potential infringement involving Universal Robots.

In a Sept. 3 statement, JAKA said its legal advisers had verified that, as of Sept. 2, “no court proceedings” concerning the alleged infringement had been filed or opened against JAKA. It also said it had received no legal documents or court notification. The discrepancy could simply be the timeframe between filing a case with the court and formally notifying or serving the defendant.

The docket currently lists 128 documents, but the filings remain unavailable to the public.

This lawsuit is Teradyne Robotics’ second major case involving a Chinese robotics company in Europe this year. In February 2026, the company sued Elite Robots’ German subsidiary over alleged copyright infringement.

Editor’s note: James Davidson, chief AI officer at Teradyne Robotics, will speak at RoboBusiness 2026. The event takes place Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif., and attract 1,500+ attends from the robotics development community. Register now to attend.

The post Teradyne Robotics sues JAKA over 3 Universal Robots patents appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Swarmer to acquire Ukrainian UGV maker Ratel Robotics for up to $224M
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
Swarmer, which has developed swarm software, plans to work with Ratel Robotics' unmanned ground vehicles in Ukraine.

The post Swarmer to acquire Ukrainian UGV maker Ratel Robotics for up to $224M appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Ratel Robotics makes uncrewed ground vehicles for Ukrainian defense. Credit: Viktor Kharyton, Swarmer

Ukrainian companies have demonstrated their ability to develop and field autonomous systems at a fraction of the price of Western defense contractors, according to Swarmer Inc. The company today said it has signed an agreement to acquire Ratel Robotics, a leading manufacturer of uncrewed ground vehicles or UGVs.

“Ratel is a major provider of UGVs for Ukraine,” stated Alex Fink, co-founder, president, and U.S. CEO of Swarmer. “Combining a battle-tested launch platform with our combat-proven autonomy software is the key to creating versatile, interoperable solutions. We are excited to have [CEO] Taras Ostapchuk and his team at Ratel Robotics be the first to join Swarmer and grow our business in Ukraine and beyond.”

Founded in 2023, Swarmer said it specializes in vendor-agnostic software that allows one operator to control hundreds of autonomous platforms in real time. The Austin, Texas-based company‘s primary mission areas include autonomous swarm coordination, integration of multi-domain unmanned systems, and AI-powered autonomy software for distributed operations.

Swarmer said its intelligence layer enables large numbers of low-cost drones and robots to operate as a coherent, resilient force. The company claimed that its technology has been validated in real battlefields, with first deployments in combat operations in Ukraine in April 2024.

Since then, Swarmer said it has completed more than 100,000 combat missions, generating terabytes of proprietary data to refine its machine-learning models and enable the replication of advanced pilot performance at scale. The company maintains operations and teams in Ukraine, Poland, and Estonia.

Editor’s note: Field robotics is among the session track topics at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Ratel Robotics develops robots for dangerous missions

“Having served in the armed forces of Ukraine, I understand firsthand the risks soldiers face on the battlefield,” said Ostapchuk. “That experience inspired me to create robotic systems capable of taking on the most dangerous missions and protecting human lives.

Ratel Robotics has developed systems to support Ukrainian Defense Forces since 2023. The Kyiv, Ukraine-based company‘s UGVs perform battlefield logistics, casualty evacuation, reconnaissance, de-mining, strike, and drone-launch missions.

Ratel is also developing an integrated autonomy ecosystem, including two uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) variants, mobile workshops, and solar-powered trailers.

“Together with Swarmer, we plan to combine ground capabilities and aerial capabilities with increasing levels of autonomy,” said Ostapchuk. “This is the next stage in the evolution of modern warfare – putting fewer people in harm’s way and having more unmanned assets take on the risk.”

The company noted that it is working with international partners. It said that every serial Ratel H and Ratel M model it produces carries a NATO stock number under the NCAGE Code A3X8J as well as an AQAP 2110 certificate, the NATO standard for quality assurance throughout design, development, and production.

Ratel has secured contracts totaling $86 million this year, and it is in discussions with multiple NATO nations under the “Build With Ukraine” initiative.

The company’s products account for about 37% of the entire 11 billion UAH ($246.85 million U.S.) spent by the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense Procurement Agency on UGVs from Jan. 1 to April 18, 2026. Those contracts will be unaffected by the acquisition, said Fink.

“They’re almost unique in the space because they have no salespeople, no government relations, no lobbying,” he noted about Ratel Robotics. “All of their sales are essentially driven by the combat units wanting their products because they are secure.”

Fink said during a press call that Swarmer was interested in Ratel because it could use UGVs to launch drones, interceptors, and swarm defense systems.

“We think that this unlocks the ability to run much larger swarmers in much larger quantities,” he asserted. “Our software already supports up to 690 drones per swarm. This allows the units to set them up fast enough to be able to launch this many as well.”

Swarmer is building a platform for battle-tested products

“In my recent letter to shareholders, I stated our objective to build a platform company for products that have been tested on the battlefield and proven effective under the most demanding operational conditions,” said Erik Prince, Swarmer’s chairman of the board. “Ratel precisely fits that mission. I believe Swarmer can accelerate its capabilities, scale its reach and integrate it with other proven technologies.”

The acquisition will include a mix of cash and stock worth up to $224 million if all earnout milestones are met, said Swarmer. Closing remains subject to customary conditions and any required legal, regulatory, and shareholder approvals.

Ratel Robotics said it expects its more than 300 employees to join Swarmer upon closing, bringing the total company’s size to nearly 500 people. Ostapchuk will continue in his role as CEO of Ratel Robotics as a wholly owned subsidiary and will report directly to Fink.

“We are potentially a vehicle for companies that have great technology to immediately pair that with a marketing machine, sales teams on three different continents, a compliance apparatus, and a way to raise more funds,” said Fink. “Because in many cases, when you grow as fast as these companies are growing, then you need working capital to actually be able to buy the parts ahead of manufacturing. And we have access to the U.S. capital markets. So as long as the orders are coming, we can help accelerate the growth for companies like this.”

The acquisition would also result in a diversified supply chain beyond Ukraine, added Prince, who acknowledged that Swarmer is looking for other defensive and offensive acquisitions.

“Ukrainians have figured out how to wage war at an innovative, low-cost way, vastly superior to what the Western defense cartel has been able to do,” said Prince. “The job is to convert that knowledge and that cost-effectiveness into a sustainable, profitable, war-winning enterprise.”

A year ago, the Ukrainian parent of Swarmer itself raised $15 million in Series A funding led by U.S. investors.

Other noteworthy defense robotics investments this year include Saronic’s $1.75 billion Series D, Hadrian’s $1.37 billion, Mach Industries‘ $600 million, and Shield AI’s $500 million. Crunchbase estimated that $14.6 billion had been invested military, national security, and law enforcement companies as of June 2, compared with $9.6 billion in all of 2025.

“Every company in the space that I know of has grown more than 5x this year,” said Fink. He told The Robot Report that Swarmer cannot make plans to integrate drone swarms and Ratel’s UGV technologies until the deal has been approved.

The post Swarmer to acquire Ukrainian UGV maker Ratel Robotics for up to $224M appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Comau automates picking, handling, and palletizing for Decathlon
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Comau's system incorporates its MyCo cobot, ROS2 software architecture, AI-powered vision systems, and a modular gripper.

The post Comau automates picking, handling, and palletizing for Decathlon appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Comau designed its MyCo family of cobots for quick installation, easy programming, and rapid redeployment. | Source: Comau

Comau SpA yesterday said it has designed and validated an order-preparation system tested in Decathlon’s e-commerce fulfillment operations. The system is part of MASTERLY, a European initiative designed to accelerate the transition from traditional mass production to highly flexible, customized manufacturing systems.

The system uses the Turin, Italy-based company‘s MyCo collaborative robot with a ROS 2-based software architecture. It integrates an advanced modular gripper to autonomously manage picking, handling, and palletizing tasks across variable product flows.

“Comau’s role in the MASTERLY project is fully aligned with our commitment to advancing next-generation manufacturing by promoting reconfigurability, efficiency, and human-centric automation,” said Alessandro Piscioneri, the head of product and solution management of advanced automation solutions at Comau.

“The project also highlights the strategic value of combining intelligent robotics, digital technologies and systems integration to create highly flexible logistics and fulfillment operations capable of adapting to rapidly changing production and market demands while maintaining operational continuity, scalability and ease of use,” he stated. “Comau’s growing strategic focus on intralogistics includes strengthening our capabilities through acquisitions, including Automha and Invent, which enable us to deliver increasingly integrated and intelligent solutions across the entire warehouse and production value chain.”

Comau designs system for complex fulfillment

Comau said it engineered MyCo to manipulate objects varying in shape, weight, and material. In addition to MyCo, the solution also incorporates advanced sensors, vision-based object recognition, digital twin capabilities, and workflow orchestration tools.

The company said the system can manage the rigid, soft, and porous materials commonly found in e-commerce fulfillment environments. Comau also claimed that its system enables real-time optimization and smooth interaction between operators and the automated processes. This helps it ensure high flexibility while maintaining consistent throughput and operational reliability, it said.

Comau said the knowledge gained and functionalities validated during the project will contribute to the continued evolution of its MyCo platform. The company said it expects these improvements to become part of its broader portfolio of advanced intralogistics capabilities.

MASTERLY uses AI, automation for supply chain resilience

Comau noted that its role within the MASTERLY project reflects its use of advanced AI-backed automation to address evolving production challenges. This includes increasing variability, supply chain disruptions, and the need for rapid reconfiguration.

The company acknowledged that it developed the intelligent warehousing and logistics system with the project’s ecosystem of technology partners. Comau said its scalable and versatile automation is designed to improve workplace ergonomics, reduce physical strain, and enhance operational flexibility within human-centric production environments.

The project parameters were driven by Decathlon’s operational requirements within the targeted fulfillment process, which has provided the foundation for implementing and validating several advanced functionalities. Key partners included Decathlon itself and STAM, a Genoa-based systems integrator, alongside the broader MASTERLY consortium.

Decathlon has worked with other robotics companies, including Exotec, Geek+, PAL Robotics, and Simbe Robotics.

item.title: What bricklaying has taught Monumental about robots in construction
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
The construction industry is rife with opportunity for robotics, but the technology hasn't broken in at scale yet.

The post What bricklaying has taught Monumental about robots in construction appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Monumental’s Pisa robot, which is in charge of laying bricks and mortar. | Source: Monumental

Currently, 92% of contractors have a difficult time filling roles in construction, according to the Association of General Contractors. At the same time, the U.S. is short 4.5 million homes. Developers like Monumental are betting on robots to help bridge this gap.

Construction’s labor issues will only continue to get worse, assuming the current trends continue. More and more people are retiring from the industry, while fewer young people are interested in getting into it. Salar al Khafaji, the founder and CEO of Monumental, believes construction’s labor shortage presents a unique opportunity for robotics.

“Construction is a really interesting use case for robots and AI, because it’s one of the few industries where the narrative is really not AI and robots coming in to replace labor to make things cheaper or redundant,” al Khafaji told The Robot Report. “It’s literally there’s not enough people to do the work. We desperately need this technology.”

Monumental is developing a fleet of robots that can handle construction tasks. The company decided to start with bricklaying for two main reasons. The first is because bricklaying is difficult work, said al Khafaji. He said he believes if the team can automate this task, it can likely take on a range of other tasks on a construction site.

The second reason goes back to labor. “If you look at Western Europe, bricklayers are literally the No. 1 job-shortage category in multiple countries, like the U.K., the Netherlands, and Germany,” al Khafaji said.

The three stages of construction, and where robotics is seeing traction

You can break down the construction process of a typical home into three major stages, al Khafaji said. The first is in ground preparation, where you use excavators and ground movers to build the foundation of a building. This is the stage where we have seen the most momentum for robotics so far.

“We’re seeing a lot of autonomous construction robotics companies that are doing excavators, ground movers, Caterpillar-like machines,” al Khafaji said. “These are heavy machines, they’re not precise.”

In this stage, there are companies like Bedrock Robotics, Gravis Robotics, TerraFirma, HIVE, Built Robotics, and more. These companies have seen some large funding round recently, including $200 million for Gravis Robotics, $115 million for TerraFirma, and $270 million for Bedrock Robotics.

Monumental doesn’t see these companies as its competitors, as it works in the second phase of construction, building the shell. “We want to do brickwork, but also block work and other things just to build our shell,” al Khafaji said. “That’s where I actually see not a lot of competition today.”

Then there is the finishing phase, where you have to put up drywall, lay flooring, and do all the things that turn a shell of a building into a home. This category, al Khafaji said, has had even less interest from robotics. There was Canvas Robotics, which created drywall finishing robots. The company’s core technology was acquired by Oshkosh at the start of this year.

Much of construction work boils down to material handling

Monumental has built three robots to handle the bricklaying process on construction sites.

“The main robot that you can see in our videos is called Pisa. That the pick and place and the bricklaying robot. It has two tiny tower cranes, basically with two arms. It’s non-humanoid,” al Khafaji said. Pisa has one arm that picks and places the bricks while the other extrudes mortar to place in between the bricks.

The other two robots on the site are in charge of making sure Pisa has enough bricks and mortar to keep working. One, Petra, brings bricks, while the other, Panama, supplies mortar.

“A lot of things in construction actually are about material handling,” al Khafaji said. “If you go observe construction workers, you see them with wheelbarrows moving around material all the time. Solving material handling is really important on a construction site.”

Monumental’s three robots are built on the same platform, which opens the door to adding more robots to the fleet in the future. al Khafaji estimated that only 10% of the technology the company is building is strictly related to brick-laying. The other 90% is technology that is more generally related to operating a robot in a construction site.

Additionally, the team uses Pathion, a mushroom-shaped device, to help the robots communicate. The company puts one or more at a worksite and it provides 4G, 5G, Starlink computes, and Wi-Fi.

How do you navigate a fragmented industry?

On any one construction site, there could be upwards of a dozen subcontractors working together to make a final product. This makes the industry very fragmented, which can be an advantage and a disadvantage. Monumental navigates this by acting as another subcontractor on the site, it just shows up with a team of robots instead of people.

“In other industries, you actually might struggle, because you have to deeply integrate into some enterprise customers,” al Khafaji said. For example, if you want to sell to a large automotive company, you’re going to have to integrate into its existing infrastructure.

“No one is vertically integrated. It is fragmented,” al Khafaji said. “So, they’re used to, if I need this thing to be done, I need foundations to be poured, or plumbing to be done, I’m just going to call up this company, and they’re going to send a couple of dudes, and they’re just going to do the thing. That’s how they operate. No one expects that subcontractor to follow their playbook.”

But there are challenges that come with working on a site with a range of subcontractors. Challenges that any subcontractor, robotic or not, would have to grapple with.

“The challenges basically have to do with all the dependencies,” al Khafaji said. “You can do everything right, but if you show up and the bricks were not delivered, you’re not going to lay bricks. It doesn’t really matter how good your robots are.”

There are some companies, like Reframe Systems, that are taking a completely different approach. Instead of acting as a contractor, Reframe seeks to build entire homes using its robotic microfactories.

Learning from deployments will be key to scaling

So far, Monumental has learned its biggest lessons from being out in the field deploying its robots. The company prioritized getting deployments in its first year of operation.

“We’ve always said we don’t want to be a robotics lab where we build stuff that doesn’t touch the reality for a year or something like that,” al Khafaji said.

On site, the team has come across scenarios it could spend years trying to predict and plan for. For example, al Khafaji said, before its early deployments, the team had spent a lot of time training its computer vision models to recognize bricks, which are similarly shaped but not completely uniform.

“We use computer vision models to measure them, to identify them, to look at the corners,” al Khafaji said. “There’s all this stuff happening, and we only heard a couple weeks before that deployment that the bricks that were going to be used were pitch black bricks, absolutely pitch black. I’d never seen them before.”

The model, which had been trained on the typical red bricks and some other lighter colors, was not able to recognize the black ones. The team had to retrain it to be able to handle the job. “We got new data. This is actually why it’s great to do these deployments. You get real-world data,” al Khafaji said.

Right now, the robotic construction industry is generally in the small pilots stage, which is really a learning stage, al Khafaji said.

“You need more examples of brick colors, weather, construction size, different regions, different countries, different regulations. Then you build a data set rich enough where you can 10x now, we can 100x now, and it’s not going to break apart. We understand the edge cases,” al Khafaji said.

al Khafaji asserted that it’s more of a matter of time and getting the work done and said he believes robots will only continue growing in construction.

The post What bricklaying has taught Monumental about robots in construction appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Unitree shares down 53% from IPO debut
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
The market is pulling back on Unitree's $66 billion valuation from its debut on the Shanghai Stock Exchange just last month.

The post Unitree shares down 53% from IPO debut appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Unitree offers its G1 humanoid robot for $13.5K. | Source: Unitree

Shares of Unitree Robotics have fallen nearly 40% from their first-day closing price on Aug. 19 2026, erasing roughly $20 billion in market value from that point and about $35 billion from their peak.

The Hangzhou, China-based company, trading on the Shanghai Stock Exchange under Ticker 688836, closed Wednesday at 513.93 yuan ($72.10 U.S.). That’s down about 39% from its 845-yuan closing price on debut and about 53% below its first-day high of 1,100 yuan.

Unitree shares are still more than three times higher than its 150.80-yuan IPO price.

The legged robot developer raised about 6.1 billion yuan ($900 million) in its IPO and saw its shares soar 460% on the first day of trading. The stock briefly climbed as high as 1,100 yuan, pushing Unitree’s valuation to nearly 445 billion yuan, or roughly $66 billion.

Before the IPO, Unitree had targeted a valuation of roughly 42 billion yuan ($6.2 billion). It ultimately priced the offering at 150.80 yuan per share, valuing the company at about 61 billion yuan ($9 billion).

The subsequent decline doesn’t necessarily mean investors have lost faith in Unitree. It suggests that the market may be pulling back from the crazy initial valuation.

Unitree has the revenue

Unlike many of its Western humanoid competitors, Unitree isn’t a pre-revenue startup waiting to prove that customers will pay for its robots. The company generated 1.70 billion yuan ($252 million) in revenue in 2025, up from 392.77 million yuan in 2024. It sells humanoids, quadrupeds, and various components.

Humanoid robots are also becoming a major part of that business. Revenue from humanoid robots reached 868 million yuan in 2025, or 51.78% of total revenue. Unitree shipped more than 5,500 humanoids during the year.

Revenue continued to grow rapidly in 2026. Unitree projected first-half revenue of between 1.052 billion and 1.128 billion yuan, representing year-over-year growth of roughly 36% to 45%.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

So the issue isn’t whether Unitree has a real business. It does. At Wednesday’s close, Unitree was worth roughly $30 billion. That’s roughly 125 times its 2025 revenue and more than 350 times its adjusted 2025 earnings. At its peak valuation of roughly $66 billion, Unitree was worth more than 250 times its 2025 revenue. That’s an extraordinary valuation.

China starting to worry about humanoid hype?

Unitree’s stock slide is also happening as Chinese regulators reportedly become more cautious about humanoid companies trying to go public.

According to The Information, the China Securities Regulatory Commission has informally raised the bar for humanoid IPO candidates. Regulators have told some investment banks and companies that prospective listings should demonstrate recurring revenue, progress toward reducing losses or significant technological innovation. Reuters could not independently verify the report, and Chinese financial regulators have not commented.

The Wall Street Journal separately reported that Chinese regulators have informally signaled that humanoid companies seeking to list should demonstrate stronger financials, revenue potential and genuine technological innovation.

Unitree’s stock performance since debuting on Shanghai’s STAR Market in August 2026.

That scrutiny is notable because Unitree’s revenue is already substantial. The question is what that revenue represents and how much of the humanoid market is coming from repeatable deployments.

The Wall Street Journal said that less than 10% of Unitree’s 2025 revenue came from industrial applications. More than 40% of Unitree’s total 2025 revenue came from overseas, meaning roughly 60% was domestic.

The Financial Times has reported that China has established more than 90 humanoid training centers, many of which are co-funded by local governments and robot manufacturers. These centers buy humanoids and use them to generate training data, often through teleoperation.

Another reality check

Unitree’s financial performance becomes even more interesting when compared with the financials of other humanoid developers, particularly those based in the U.S. that are trying to deploy humanoids in industrial settings. Oregon-based Agility Robotics, for example, recently opened its books for the first time as part of its proposed SPAC with Churchill Capital Corp. XI.

According to its S-4 filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Agility generated $1.78 million in net sales in 2025. At the same time, it recorded a $140.2 million operating loss and a $138.1 million net loss. The company spent about $91.6 million on R&D and ended the year with roughly $103 million in cash.

We don’t have comparable revenue figures for other leading U.S.-based humanoid developers such as 1X Technologies, Apptronik or Figure. Boston Dynamics‘ revenue, meanwhile, comes primarily from its Spot quadruped and Stretch trailer-unloading robots, not its Atlas humanoid. If we did, they’d also be low.

Low revenue numbers aren’t surprising for companies trying to commercialize industrial humanoids. Agility said its Digit robots have been deployed at 9 customer sites and have accumulated more than 65,000 operating hours. The company also said it has more than $300 million in multi-year contracted Digit v5 orders.

The proposed SPAC transaction values Agility at about $2.5 billion, roughly 1,400 times its 2025 net sales. Unitree, meanwhile, is worth roughly $30 billion despite generating hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue and turning a profit.

Agility and others are still trying to prove that humanoids can generate meaningful revenue from industry. Unitree has shown the revenue. Now the market wants to know how much more of it is coming, where it’s coming from, and how much today’s valuation is already pricing in.

item.title: AGIBOT to explain how to scale humanoids from the lab to the real world at RoboBusiness
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
AGIBOT plans to give attendees actionable insights on identifying high-value robotics use cases and building sustainable developer ecosystems.

The post AGIBOT to explain how to scale humanoids from the lab to the real world at RoboBusiness appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
AGIBOT’s semi-humanoid robot working in a pilot at Longcheer Technology’s Nanchang factory. | Source: AGIBOT

While generative AI has redefined the digital world, the true frontier lies in the physical realm in translating embodied AI into scalable, commercial reality. For global enterprises and scaling startups alike, the bottleneck is no longer just algorithm training. The bottleneck is the systemic deployment of hardware capable of execution in complex human environments.

At RoboBusiness 2026, Yinghao Song, the head of North America and product lead at AGIBOT, will talk about “Scaling Humanoids from Lab to Real-World Deployment.” The event will take place on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Song will give his talk on the first day of the show at 1:15 p.m. PT.

In this session, Song will break down the strategic blueprint for taking advanced robotics from pilot projects to global go-to-market (GTM) execution. He will draw from his company‘s experience with rapid scaling and discuss:

  • The unique investment logic driving the humanoid and quadruped sectors
  • The core supply chain dynamics required to achieve mass-production inflection points
  • The return on investment (ROI) frameworks that enterprises demand before integration.

Yinghao will also address the critical “software-hardware gap.” He will explain how modular software stacks and open software development kits (SDKs) empower partners to deploy full-size humanoids and highly dexterous hands across automotive, manufacturing, logistics, and unstructured research environments.

Attendees will gain actionable insights on identifying high-value robotics use cases, building sustainable developer ecosystems, and mastering the cross-border scaling strategies necessary to win in the 2026 embodied AI landscape.

AGIBOT is a global developer in embodied AI and full-spectrum robotic systems. Yinghao has an MBA from the Kellogg School of Management at Northwestern University, melding technical acumen with commercial strategy for industrial hardware and software.

He orchestrates AGIBOT’s international GTM execution, product positioning, and developer ecosystem architecture. Yinghao said he focuses on accelerating the commercial deployment of full-size humanoids, advanced quadrupeds, and dexterous robotic hands across industrial and research sectors, bridging the gap between cutting-edge intelligence and enterprise-grade scaling.

item.title: Vention opens Physical AI Lab for manufacturing in Montreal
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
Vention's new Physical AI Lab will focus on advancing robotic manipulation from research to scalable production-line deployment.

The post Vention opens Physical AI Lab for manufacturing in Montreal appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Vention and its partners have invested in space and equipment for its new physical AI lab. Source: Vention

To generate high-quality data for training the AI models that operate next-generation robots, you need scale. Vention Inc. today opened its Physical AI Lab in Montreal. The company said the new laboratory focuses on robotic manipulation in manufacturing.

“Any physical AI foundation model is data-hungry,” Etienne Lacroix, founder and CEO of Vention, told The Robot Report. “We move several hundred robot cells a year, and they all collect high-quality industrial manipulation data. It was a massive asset that was not properly leveraged until now.”

Vention said its technology stack includes hardware, software, and physical AI. The Montreal-based company claimed that it enables businesses to design, program, and deploy turnkey or custom automation in days. It has deployed more than 28,000 machines worldwide and a community of more than 6,000 factories.

Vention addresses manufacturing challenges

With its technology deployed across manufacturers globally, including 90 of the Fortune 500, Vention said its scale gives researchers direct access to real environments and a continuous stream of data to post-train physical AI models.

“Physical AI will fundamentally expand what manufacturers can automate, but the challenge is no longer simply proving that a robot can perform a task in a lab,” stated Lacroix. “The real opportunity is making these capabilities reliable, economical, and deployable across thousands of factories. By combining Canada’s world-class AI ecosystem with Vention’s deep robotics expertise, industrial data, and full-stack automation platform, we have a unique foundation to close that gap.”

Revenue related to physical AI has increased by 400% over the past year, reported Vention. The company’s mandate is to enable scalable deployment by validating new AI capabilities against the reliability, cost, and variability requirements of real production lines.

“We know about Skild, Generalist, and Physical Intelligence — there are many models and policies,” Lacroix observed. “The base model is not the problem; some models are better for certain tasks. We can add value and shape the research agenda with efficient learning, data collection, and post-training capabilities.”

Editor’s note: Physical AI is among the session topic tracks at RoboBusiness 2026, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. Register now to attend.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

Physical AI Lab takes research to the factory floor

Vention said its new lab includes industrial data collection, robotics control, motion planning, classical computer vision, vision foundation models, learning from demonstration, and reinforcement learning. It focuses on complex and unstructured manufacturing tasks.

The company noted that while model development is shaped by research and benchmarks, it also relies on industry feedback and day-to-day deployment conversations.

“What makes this lab different is the loop we’ve built: academic research feeding directly into live production problems, and production feedback feeding back into the research,” said Dr. Jimmy Li, director of physical AI at Vention. “Our clients aren’t waiting for a finished product to test; they’re in the room while we build it. That’s unique in this field, and it’s what lets us move faster from a research result to something that actually runs on a factory floor.”

Li, head of Vention’s Physical AI Lab, is a robotics and machine learning researcher from McGill University who has more than a decade of experience with peer-reviewed research in computer vision, robot perception, autonomous systems, and AI-powered robotic manipulation. Over the past two years, he has led Vention’s physical AI strategy and its collaboration with NVIDIA, translating advances in AI research into commercial robotic applications.

Jimmy Li, director of the new Physical AI Lab in Montreal. Source: Vention

Innovation under way for industrial applications

Vention said its new lab has already generated new intellectual property and plans to continue to do so. It launched GRIIP (Generalized Robotic Industrial Intelligence Pipeline) in February 2026. The modular physical AI pipeline spans scene digitalization, object segmentation, pose estimation, grasp selection, and collision-free motion planning.

GRIIP uses foundation models from technology leaders such as NVIDIA as well as Vention’s proprietary models. The company plans to release a public GRIIP Software Development Kit (SDK).

“We will put GRIIP in open source and show it alongside our other AI-defined automation at IMTS,” said Lacroix. Vention plans to introduce physical AI and agentic AI capabilities unified in a single platform.

The company is also working with global industrial and electronics manufacturers, including a large automotive OEM on high-complexity, unstructured robotic tasks in final assembly.

“We’ve always been in applied use cases, learning from demonstrations and data collection, using tens of millions of dollars in R&D, and fine-fine tuning models for industrial automation,” said Lacroix. “Kitting is one of our top applied research use cases, which is horizontal — it’s in automotive, in aerospace, and in consumer.”

“Electronics contract manufacturers have all those pieces of hardware coming from various vendors and various packaging, They need to be opened and reassembled into a kit that will go at a specific station on the assembly line,” he explained. “If you’re a car manufacturer, it could be headlamps with a harness, a mounting bracket, and a screw, and they need to be prepared so Position 7 on the line has the right kit for the right car. Kitting was a use case where those new class of policies are relevant.”

External advisor brings connections to physical AI community

In addition, Vention named Dr. Joelle Pineau, chief AI officer at Cohere, as external technical advisor for the Physical AI Lab. She will contribute to model architecture decisions, research prioritization, and connections into the broader AI community.

“Dr. Pineau was a former VP of research at Meta, and she did her Ph.D. at CMU,” said Lacroix. “She managed the teams that developed the SAM 2 model for segmentation.”

As foundation models mature, Vention said it expects the complexity and costs of deploying robots to drop, widening the range of manufacturers that can put them to work.

The post Vention opens Physical AI Lab for manufacturing in Montreal appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Boston Dynamics veteran launches Dynamic Creatures to bring characters to life with robotics
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Dynamic Creatures plants to create its own line of characters, and to re-create characters for specific brands and environments.

The post Boston Dynamics veteran launches Dynamic Creatures to bring characters to life with robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Dynamic Creatures co-founder and CEO Marc Theermann (left) and co-founder and CTO Farbod Farshidian. | Source: Dynamic Creatures | Source: Dynamic Creatures

Boston Dynamics is focused on commercializing robots for industrial work, but it’s always had time for some fun, too. We’ve seen Spot and Atlas dance, flip, compete on America’s Got Talent, take part in the FIFA World Cup, and more. Now, two Boston Dynamics veterans are launching Dynamic Creatures. The new company is focused on creating robotic characters for entertainment. 

Dynamic Creatures was co-founded by CEO Marc Theermann, former chief strategy officer at Boston Dynamics, and CTO Farbod Farshidian, former research leader at the Robotics and AI Institute. Theermann told The Robot Report the name company name pays homage to Boston Dynamics and Jim Henson’s Creature Shop.

“We always put out those videos, A, because it’s super fun, and B, because we wanted to bring the general public along,” Theermann said. “We always thought that, ultimately, these robots are going to be everywhere in our daily lives, so we wanted to show these robots in these fun environments, just to make sure that people understand the capabilities of these robots in terms of their abilities to locomote.”

With these videos and excursions, Theermann began seeing interest in robots for entertainment. “Humans love to see robots dancing and love to see robots in these fun environments,” Theermann said. 

Dynamic Creatures is targeting a range of entertainment use cases at theme parks, casinos, cruise shapes, and hospitality settings. It is also Boston Dynamics’ official entertainment and hospitality partner.

“Dynamic Creatures is opening an important new frontier for advanced robotics,” said Amanda McMaster, the Interim CEO of Boston Dynamics. “As our official entertainment and hospitality partner, the company is combining proven robotic platforms with character design, adaptive behavior and real-time interaction to create experiences the market has not had access to before. Marc and Farbod bring the rare combination of commercial and technical expertise required to turn that vision into compelling, guest-facing systems.”

Dynamic Creatures is backed by a mix of U.S. and European institutional investors. These include Eniac Ventures, Kindred Ventures, Heliad, Sunshine Lake and BlueGrass Ventures, along with strategic angel investors Marc Raibert, the executive director of the RAI Institute and founder of Boston Dynamics, and Lukas Ziegler. 

Dynamic Creatures launches SnowJay

Dynamic Creatures introduced SnowJay, its integrated AI and robotics platform. This serves as the operating layer for the company’s robots. Theermann said the platform is in charge of two main things: natural movement and human-robot interaction.

“One of the cores of our platform is that we can make any robot walk in these very natural ways,” Theermann said. “The way that we do it is either through motion capture or through animations, where we use NVIDIA tools and reinforcement learning to teach these robots these organic behaviors.”

Theermann said most of the locomotion work is led by Farshidian, who helped to give Atlas a more natural gait during its debut at CES 2026.

“If you look at many robots out there, they’re deaf and mute. We think that in order for robots to be accepted into society, in restaurants and in general spaces outside, they need to be better at human-robot interaction,” Theermann said. “In robotics, at the moment, everybody is talking about vision learning action models, where something happens to the robot. The robot processes that input and then reacts with an output. Lots of people are focused on dexterous manipulation as the next big hurdle in robotics, which is certainly super important, but that’s not what we’re focused on. We’re focused on human-robot interaction as the output.” 

What kind of characters will Dynamic Creatures create?

Dynamic Creatures is building on top of third-party hardware at the moment, in particular Boston Dynamics’ Spot quadruped and Atlas humanoid. However, the company’s technology is also compatible with Unitree robots. “We do have ambitions to build our own humanoid hardware. We want to become a full stack robotics company,” Theermann said. 

Dynamic Creatures has two prototype characters that it has developed in-house. One, shown in its launch video, is a purple poodle named Danielle. It’s also working on a Tyrolean mountain troll, Theermann said, similar to a Yeti.

However, the company’s first two partners are looking for customer characters from famous IP.

“The partnerships that we are currently working on are partners coming to us with their IP and saying, ‘Can you bring my IP to life? I have an IP already from a movie or from a TV show, can you bring that IP to life in my theme park or for my red carpet event?’” Theermann said.

Managed pilots in 2027

For its early deployments, Dynamic Creatures said it will be using operators to control the robots, allowing them to gather critical data to train its model. Theermann said this kind of data can only be collected by interacting with humans, which is why hospitality and events are so important.

“We can have these interactions with humans and really start to understand what makes people laugh, what gets a chuckle out of them, how do they react to a robot when the robot does certain things. That’s really what we’re setting out to learn over the next couple of years with this platform,” Theermann said. 

“We want to become the best at human-robot interaction. At the moment, we’ve actually hired puppeteers to help us figure out different emotions for our robot to see what works and what doesn’t work,” he continued.

Dynamic Creatures hopes to have its first customer deployments in early 2027. These will start out with a mixture of teleoperation and autonomy, which they call assisted autonomy.

“It will be managed pilots. We will send humans and robots, and we will closely monitor what happens so we can learn together with our clients,” Theermann said. “In our case, it might be assisted autonomy, plus puppeteering. Then, over time, hopefully you go from teleoperation to telemonitoring, and then telemonitoring offsite. At the same time, the relationship of operator to robot goes from one-to-one to one-to-many.” 

Theermann said, alongside human-robot collaboration, safety and semantic navigation are the big research thrusts for the company. 

“Humanoid robot safety hasn’t fully been figured out yet. Right now, in factory environments, deployed humanoid robots typically are behind a light curtain. When a human walks through the light curtain, the robot slows down and then fully stops. We want to get to a point where you can hug the robot,” Theermann said. “We need to approach safety from a totally different viewpoint.” 

The post Boston Dynamics veteran launches Dynamic Creatures to bring characters to life with robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: AI can’t outrun a humanoid’s hardware
item.dc:creator: Andreas P. Friedrich
item.description:
The remarkable progress in AI has brought robotics closer to machines capable of determining what they should do. The next major advance may depend on whether their physical systems can execute those decisions efficiently, precisely and safely.

The post AI can’t outrun a humanoid’s hardware appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Editor’s note: Andreas Friedrich, managing director technology and strategy, Allegro MicroSystems, will be speaking at RoboBusiness, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif. He will dissect the critical technological advancements that are making next-generation robotic actuation possible. Register for RoboBusiness today. The Robot Report and parent company Arrowfly produce the event.

The more capable a humanoid robot becomes, the more difficult it is to accommodate the hardware required to make it move. The humanoid environment is one of articulated joints and degrees of freedom, where hardware faces stringent size and weight constraints, and motion requires a slew of motors, sensing, control, power and safety systems.

Artificial intelligence has helped humanoids better perceive their surroundings, interpret instructions and determine what actions to take. Translating those decisions into precise, fluid and safe physical movement presents a different engineering challenge.

That distinction matters more as humanoids move from laboratory prototypes to practical machines capable of operating alongside people. Continued advances in AI matter, but the physical limits of the robot determine how that intelligence is put to work.

From fixed automation to autonomous machines

Consider the difference between a traditional industrial robot and a humanoid. An industrial robotic arm may have six or seven axes and spend its entire working life bolted to a factory floor. Weight at its base may matter relatively little. Thick copper cables can deliver power. Motor drives can be housed outside the robot in control cabinets. If necessary, the system can accommodate substantial cooling infrastructure.

A humanoid with 30 or more degrees of freedom has none of those luxuries. Every additional joint introduces another combination of motors, power electronics, position and current sensing, control and safety functions. All of that hardware has to travel with the robot. Every gram contributes to the energy required to move it, and every millimeter occupied by electronics competes for space inside an arm, leg, hand or finger.

The electronics required to give a humanoid freedom of movement take up precious space and add weight that can actually restrict how freely the robot moves. This engineering paradox is particularly acute in dexterous hands, where multiple motors, sensors and control functions must fit into extremely tight spaces, making the joint itself a system-level design problem.

Register now and help us celebrate 20 years of RoboBusiness!

When power architecture determines mobility

The evolving power architecture of advanced robots demonstrates how closely electrical and mechanical design are connected. Early robotic systems were commonly designed around relatively low-voltage power distribution. More advanced mobile robots and humanoids are moving toward higher voltages, specifically 48V DC architectures.

Physics explains why. For the same amount of delivered power, moving from 12V to 48V reduces the required current by a factor of four. Designers can use thinner wiring, reducing copper weight throughout the machine. And because resistive losses scale with the square of current, reducing current by four reduces wiring losses by a factor of 16.

In a humanoid, those electrical gains have mechanical consequences. Less wiring weight reduces the energy required for movement, while lower thermal loads make it easier to package electronics into joints that cannot accommodate elaborate cooling systems.

Higher voltage, however, introduces its own engineering problem. Motors do not always consume energy. During rapid deceleration they can behave as generators, producing transient voltages considerably higher than the nominal DC bus voltage. The electronics controlling the joint must withstand those events without damage or loss of control.

Higher voltage reduces current, heat and wiring weight, but it also raises the demands placed on motor-control electronics. Changes in power, thermal performance, weight or reliability can directly affect the others. Similar tradeoffs appear throughout the humanoid.

AI can decide, but the joint still has to execute

A higher-level AI system may determine that a robot should pick up an object, turn a handle or hand someone a glass. But the instruction itself does not produce useful physical movement. Each joint must continuously determine where it is, how it is moving and how much force it is applying. Position, current and torque information feed a closed control loop that measures actual movement against commanded movement and continuously adjusts motor behavior.

Consider the seemingly simple task of handing someone a cup of tea. The robot cannot just move its arm toward a predetermined coordinate. It must know the position of its joints and control the torque being applied as the arm moves, while responding to changing physical conditions. This form of physical intelligence encompasses the sensing, actuation and feedback required to translate an AI decision into controlled movement.

More sophisticated motion also places greater demands on sensing. A shoulder and a finger, for example, have very different mechanical and packaging requirements. Large motors can create electromagnetic interference that sensing systems must tolerate, while smaller joints impose severe space limitations and still require precise position data.

No single sensing architecture is likely to address every joint. Precise, reliable feedback is part of the control loop that turns machine intelligence into physical action.

Safety moves inside the control loop

That control becomes even more consequential when robots begin working alongside people. Industrial automation environments often manage risk by separating humans and machines. A humanoid designed to collaborate with a factory worker or assist with tasks in the home cannot depend on that separation. Functional safety becomes part of the robot.

The control system must continuously monitor operating conditions, detect faults or anomalous behavior and quickly move the affected subsystem to an appropriate safe state when necessary. Building those capabilities from scratch can create hardware redundancy, software overhead and certification work.

Robotics designers can draw on engineering disciplines that have dealt with similar challenges. Automotive systems such as electronic steering and braking combine high-power electromechanical actuation with sensing, diagnostics and functional safety. Humanoids have different requirements, but the architectural lesson still applies: diagnostics, fault detection and safe-state behavior are easier to accommodate when designed into the system from the beginning rather than layered onto a finished design.

The joint becomes a system

At the scale required by advanced humanoids, sensing, motor control, power management, thermal performance and functional safety must be addressed as an integrated electromechanical subsystem capable of converting higher-level machine intelligence into controlled physical action.

Semiconductor integration can shorten the physical and electrical distances between sensing, control and actuation, reducing PCB routing complexity, thermal hotspots and parasitic effects. Robotics engineers can then dedicate more time to the software, kinematics and system behavior that differentiate the robot rather than solving lower-level electronics problems within every joint.

The joint becomes a critical interface between AI and the physical world.

From seeing and moving to feeling

Today’s humanoids use sophisticated vision systems and powerful AI models to recognize objects. But when a person grips a tool or handles a fragile object, touch and force feedback modify the movement as it occurs. We do not simply calculate the position of our fingers and execute a predetermined trajectory. We feel the object and adjust.

Replicating human-like dexterity remains a significant challenge for robotics, particularly in the hand. Integrating force and touch sensing into fingers, fingertips and other surfaces gives machines information about what happens when they make contact with the physical world and allows them to adjust their movement in response.

The remarkable progress in AI has brought robotics closer to machines capable of determining what they should do. The next major advance may depend on whether their physical systems can execute those decisions efficiently, precisely and safely.

item.title: Why vision AI is the safety backbone of the automated job site
item.dc:creator: Gary Ng
item.description:
Vision AI doesn't replace robots or human judgement; it provides the continuous perception that allows both to operate safely together.

The post Why vision AI is the safety backbone of the automated job site appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
ViAct offers viBOT, an autonomous robotic monitor for construction. | Source: viAct

Construction is entering a new era of automation. Autonomous earthmoving equipment is beginning to reshape excavation. Robotic layout systems are improving precision. Drones are inspecting hard-to-reach structures. Across the board, vision AI-powered machines are steadily moving from controlled pilots to active job sites.

The global construction robotics market is estimated to reach $3.66 billion by 2030, according to Grand View Research.

Yet the success of construction robots won’t ultimately be determined by how capable the machines become. It will depend on something far less visible: how safely frontline workers and autonomous systems can work together.

Let’s picture a mid-rise construction project. An autonomous compactor is completing its programmed route across the site while an inspection drone carries out its routine progress survey overhead. Everything is functioning exactly as designed.

Then a worker steps into the compactor’s operating zone to retrieve a dropped tool. Nothing has malfunctioned. The machine continues following its assigned task exactly as it was programmed to do.

The challenge is that the job site has changed in a matter of seconds, and safe operations now depend on recognising that change before it becomes an incident.

That layer of safety is brought by vision AI, and it’s the quiet prerequisite the industry is currently excited about.

The transition zone, not full automation, is where construction risk concentrates

OSHA’s “Fatal Four,” falls, struck-by, electrocution, and caught-in/between hazards, account for roughly 58% to 59% of U.S. construction deaths in recent years. Struck-by incidents alone kill over 100 workers annually, with large majority of these incidents involving vehicles or moving equipment.

An autonomous rover doesn’t get tired or impatient the way a skid steer operator might late in a shift. But it also has no intuition for the fact that a worker just stepped behind a stack of rebar, or that a subcontractor’s crew wandered into a zone its path planner assumed was clear five minutes ago.

This is what robotics teams need to sit with before deployment, not after. The hard case is where excavation crews, electricians, and an autonomous compactor share the same 20 acres on a site that was never built with structured sensing in mind.

This growing challenge is reflected in evolving safety standards like the ANSI/RIA R15.08. This was developed to address autonomous mobile robots operating in dynamic environments, moving beyond earlier AGV standards that assumed fixed guide paths.

Every robot sees locally. Vision AI sees the whole job site

Every autonomous machine already relies on perception. Cameras, lidar, radar, ultrasonic sensors, GPS, and onboard AI help it navigate, detect obstacles, and safely complete the task it has been assigned. These systems are exceptionally good at understanding what is happening immediately around the machine.

Construction, however, demands a much broader perspective. Workers move between trades, temporary access routes are opened, materials are relocated, and heavy equipment is redirected throughout the day. No single robot, regardless of how advanced its onboard sensors are, can understand everything happening across an entire job site.

That is where vision AI fits into the robotics ecosystem. Rather than being embedded inside one machine, vision AI acts as a site-wide perception layer. It continuously analyses live video streams from existing CCTV cameras, temporary site cameras, inspection drones, body-worn cameras, and increasingly lidar and other sensor feeds. This helps it understand how workers, vehicles, equipment, and autonomous machines are interacting in real time.

This is also starting to show up as its own category of ground-based hardware. A small but growing class of autonomous mobile patrol units like viBOT are emerging specifically to carry this perception layer physically through the site. It moves continuously through zones that fixed cameras don’t reach, and drones can’t sustain a ground-level presence in. This includes basements, tunnels, and areas that shift week to week as the work program advances.

The robot’s value isn’t the mobility itself. It’s because they extend the same vision AI layer into the blind spots between fixed infrastructure, rather than adding another isolated sensor with its own narrow field of view.

Instead of every robot operating from its own isolated field of view, vision AI creates a common operational picture of the entire site.

From seeing to understanding: The next safety layer

Vision AI is evolving beyond simply detecting hard hats or identifying exclusion zone breaches. The next generation of systems combines computer vision with agentic AI that can interpret context, reason across multiple data sources, and recommend or trigger appropriate actions in real time.

On an automated job site, this means moving from isolated alerts to coordinated decision-making. Instead of one camera flagging a worker entering a restricted zone, AI can correlate live video, equipment location, drone imagery, and site activities to understand the broader operational context.

Just as important is where this intelligence runs. Processing AI at the edge, close to the cameras and sensors, allows hazards to be identified within seconds, without relying on continuous cloud connectivity. That low-latency response is essential for active job sites where safety decisions cannot wait for data to travel to a remote server and back.

At the same time, a centralized operations dashboard provides supervisors with a single, live view of the entire site. Rather than monitoring dozens of camera feeds independently, they can understand interactions between workers, robots, vehicles, and equipment as they unfold, helping them make faster and more informed decisions.

The future of robotics starts with better awareness

Construction robotics will continue to advance rapidly over the coming decade. Machines will become more autonomous, more intelligent, and more capable of performing hazardous or repetitive work with minimal human intervention.

But automation alone will not create safer job sites. As long as humans and machines continue sharing the same workspace — and they will for many years to come — the industry needs a common understanding of what is happening across that environment in real time.

That is the role of vision AI. Not to replace robots. Not to replace human judgement. But to provide the continuous perception that allows both to operate safely together.

About the author

Gary Ng, co-founder and CEO of viAct, comes with a background of building engineering who turned into AIpreneur with inception of viAct in 2016. He has more than 10 years of experience in implementing technological innovations in construction industry.

Before viAct, Ng was the managing director of 3D fashiontech EFI Optitex. He was also recognized as the best regional senior executive in NASDAQ-listed technology enterprise Stratasys.

With his ultimate strength of analytical thinking & strategic decision making, Ng was an advisory board member for SXSV early in his career. He believes in the concept of transferring knowledge from experienced to youngsters and is a renowned academic professional. Currently a visiting faculty professional at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University. Gary is also an active public speaker and preacher of AI driven sustainability in workplaces.

item.title: Inbolt to discuss physical AI’s deployment problem at RoboBusiness
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Rudy Cohen, the co-founder and CEO of Inbolt, will reframe where physical AI pays off at RoboBusiness this fall.

The post Inbolt to discuss physical AI’s deployment problem at RoboBusiness appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Inbolt’s technology lets robots grasp parts however they can, then uses in-hand localization to adjust trajectory mid-move. | Source: Inbolt

Physical AI’s consensus says progress is gated by data. More of it, better curated, better simulated. That’s true in the lab. In the factory, it’s the wrong constraint. After deploying vision-guided control across over 100 factories and 40 million-plus robot cycles, Inbolt CEO Rudy Cohen says the real bottleneck is the loop between perception and motion, and the integration tax surrounding it.

At RoboBusiness, which will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif., Cohen will give the talk, “Physical AI Doesn’t Have a Data Problem; It Has a Deployment Problem.” The talk will take place at 2:15 p.m. on the first day of the show.

Cohn will reframe where physical AI actually pays off. Not in bigger models, but in closing the loop at servo frequency and collapsing the months of fixtures, wiring, and returning that make every deployment a six-figure project.

Using production data from lines at Stellantis, Toyota, and Ford, Cohen will make the case that physical AI is already commercially proven, just not where the headlines are looking.

About the Cohn and Inbolt

Rudy Cohen is the co-founder and CEO of Inbolt, a startup bringing vision and AI to robotics in manufacturing. He began his academic journey as a researcher in applied mathematics at École Normale Supérieure Paris-Saclay, before completing a Master’s in entrepreneurship from École Polytechnique and HEC Paris.

Inbolt is building a real-time control layer that turns digital twins into live robot execution. Since its founding in 2019, the company has raised €20 million ($23.2 million U.S.) and now operates in over 100 factories across Europe, the U.S., and Japan.
